Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Segmentation

items.reward: Walls by purpose, and a short list of doors — owned, tested and rehearsed.

items.text: Act II — “The flow that makes the show”

items.title: The flow that makes the show.
items.body: Window one, 01:00: Raffa splits control from signage. At the doors rehearsal the lobby wall doesn't switch to the countdown. The control processor sends ‘show mode’ to the players — a conversation nobody had written down, because on a flat network nobody had to. Raffa rolls back in four minutes. The walls were right. The list of doors was missing one.
items.label: Test: the flow's size — and what the window was missing.

unknown: Whether any other flow is missing

items.title: Bulkheads that stopped short
items.body: In April 1912 the largest liner afloat struck an iceberg on her maiden voyage. She had been built with watertight bulkheads dividing her hull into compartments — but they didn't reach high enough. As the bow sank, water spilled over the top of one compartment into the next, and the next. More than 1,500 people died. Compartments only protect you if the walls go all the way up.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #88 · AVERY'S LENS  Walls, and a list of doors  Segmentation is two things: segments by purpose, and a short written list of the flows allowed between them — each with an owner.  The first test window put up the walls and forgot the one door the show needed: the lobby wall stopped switching to the countdown.

items.alt: The network sheet after the fix: three boxes — CONTROL 40 with control, DSP and jump host; SIGNAGE 50 with the server and forty players; VENDOR 95 with the landing and the jump host's vendor side — joined by two short pink links; allowed flows listed: show mode from control to players on one port, vendor to jump host, jump host to control, and time; show mode rehearsed at doors.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Measure how flat it is (% = part ÷ whole × 100). Segment by purpose; then write down every flow the systems need between segments — from, to, what, why, owner — and block the rest. Cut over in windows with a tested rollback and a rehearsal of the show. The network owner builds every rule; security approves access; each flow keeps a named owner and a quarterly review.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Which conversation between your systems has nobody ever written down?
